description: We are Estudados AeroLab, first-year Computer Technician students at IFAM, with a bronze medal in the Sustainability Olympiad and participation in BIRST-OSIFOG (Brazilian Rocket Simulation Olympiad). In this hackathon, we want to learn from real NASA challenges, apply programming in practice, work as a team, and create a useful solution. Inspired by the flying rivers (Amazon moisture streams), we believe our region can reach space too, and we are ready for this mission!
summary: LabLunar is an educational simulator that runs in the browser, with no installation or sign-up. Children aged 7 to 12 manage a lunar outpost, balancing power, oxygen and radiation. Every choice has a cost: saving power at night can leave the base short of air or heat, and solar storms require sheltering. At the end, a report explains the chain of causes behind success or failure. The project addresses the challenge by turning real spacecraft constraints into playable decisions, so students learn the reasoning behind missions, not only their outcomes. It was built with HTML and JavaScript, with AI assistance for coding. Integration with NASA open data (DONKI, OSDR and Artemis) is planned, with attribution shown inside the game.
details:
What it does and how it works. Players first design a lunar outpost within a mass budget, choosing solar panels, batteries, greenhouses, water recycling and radiation shielding. The mission then runs day by day. Each day, players decide how to ration water, save energy, assign crew tasks and shelter during solar storms. The 14-day lunar night depends entirely on stored battery power. Random equipment failures add pressure, and a final post-mortem traces what caused success or failure.

Benefits. Students practise systems thinking and trade-off reasoning. Access is free and requires no account, which suits classrooms and families. Each run unfolds differently, so students can learn from failure without it feeling punitive.

Intended impact. We want children aged 7 to 12 to leave with a better understanding of what survival in space requires, and teachers to have a ready tool for discussing mission decisions. Impact is not yet measured. Testing with children is planned.

Data. The current prototype uses illustrative values. We plan to connect DONKI for real solar event data, OSDR for astronaut health and radiation findings, and Artemis or Mars mission data for environmental conditions. Each source will be credited inside the game, and each value will be referenced in the project’s data file.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in a single file. Claude (Anthropic) for design and code generation. GitHub for the repository. Google Fonts for typography. No hardware.

Creativity. The decisions are coupled. Power used at night competes with oxygen production and heating. Sheltering reduces radiation but pauses crop care. The post-mortem explains causes in plain language, instead of ending with only “game over”.

Team considerations. The team of four split the work by role: coding, scientific data, slides and video, and repository and coordination. We limited the game to a few core resources so that children are not overwhelmed. We disclose AI use in the repository. We use NASA and Space Apps logos only in their official form, without alteration.
